auxiliary_material: The text notes that the human gut microbiome is shaped by environmental exposures including diet and medication, with host genetics accounting for less than 10% of variation. This provides context for why dietary interventions are considered a viable strategy to modulate the microbiome.
outline_action: Search for publications specifically linked to the DIET trial (NCT04645680) or other registered dietary intervention trials in ICI-treated patients. Verify if the authors of this observational study have published subsequent interventional results or if a separate mediation analysis manuscript exists that fulfills the statistical mediation criterion.
remaining_gap: The success criteria require data from the DIET trial (NCT04645680) or other human dietary intervention trials. This study is explicitly observational, not an intervention trial. Furthermore, while microbiome profiling was performed, the supplied text does not report specific taxa or functional pathway changes statistically mediating the clinical efficacy in humans (it states mechanisms are unclear), nor does it contain an explicit statement that such mediation data is pending. The specific trial NCT04645680 is not mentioned.
useful_material: This study reports an observational cohort analysis (n=128 for survival analysis, n=438 for profiling) in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). The authors found that higher dietary fiber intake was associated with significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS), while the use of over-the-counter probiotic supplements was associated with impaired response. The study included fecal microbiota profiling and parallel preclinical mouse models. In mice, low-fiber diet or probiotic use led to impaired anti-PD-1 treatment response and a lower frequency of interferon-γ–positive cytotoxic T cells in the tumor microenvironment. The authors state that gut bacteria modulate ICB response but the mechanisms underlying microbiota effects are presently unclear.
